rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~90% (CME FedWatch via Hercules); ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~80%; BoJ Dec ~84%; BoC Dec ~44%; RBA 4.85%
rows.read: A December Fed hike is still seen as likely, and several officials argued for more, but the stock slide made bigger steps less likely. The European Central Bank and Bank of England are also expected to hike, while Australia's job losses make another Reserve Bank of Australia hike unlikely. US rates still look set to rise further than most, which keeps supporting the dollar.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: Australia jobs Oct −43.5K, unemployment 4.9%; UK retail sales Oct +0.7% m/m (fcst 0.0%); US UoM sentiment Nov 51.5
rows.read: Australia lost jobs for a second month, a blow to the Aussie. UK shoppers spent more than expected, partly by stocking up. A global stock slide raises worries that growth will slow, which usually hits commodity currencies hardest.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: UK CPI Oct 3.6%, core 2.8%; euro-area CPI Oct 4.0%, core 2.6%; Japan core CPI Oct 2.2%; US 1-yr inflation expectations 3.7% (prelim 4.3%)
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. UK core prices held steady while euro-area core prices firmed. US households expect a little less inflation than earlier this month, which eased bets on the Fed slightly.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: S&P 500 −3.7% Friday, >10% below Oct record; US 2-year ~4.62% (∲23bp on the week); USD/JPY −0.9% w/w; AUD/USD −2.4% w/w
rows.read: Stocks fell hard around the world last week as worries about AI spending spread, sending money into US government bonds, the yen and the franc. Over the weekend Iran struck Bahrain and more tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz, which could add to the nerves when trading reopens. The Aussie and kiwi, which suffer most when markets get nervous, start the week near multi-year lows.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Gold ~$3,524 (≈−9% w/w), low ~$3,503; Brent ~$92.82 (−3.4% w/w), WTI ~$83.94 (January contracts)
rows.read: Oil fell for a third week as Gulf supply kept flowing, which took support away from the Canadian dollar and helped energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area. Weekend attacks in the Gulf could lift oil when trading reopens. Gold's worst week in about eight months keeps weighing on the Aussie.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar after betting on it, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: US 10-year ~4.92% (−21bp on the week); ECB Financial Stability Review: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%
rows.read: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing still keeps long-term US borrowing costs high, though they slipped below 5% as money rushed into bonds during the stock slide.
